Discovering Customer Segments and Product Associations — a KDD Project¶

Author: <your name> · Course: CMPE 255 · Repo: MeronDT/CMPE-255-Data-Mining-process · App: <deployed URL>

Data: Online Retail II — UCI Machine Learning Repository (dataset 502, CC BY 4.0), donated by D. Chen. All 1,067,371 transaction lines of a UK-based online retailer of giftware (many customers are wholesalers), 1 Dec 2009 – 9 Dec 2011.

KDD (Fayyad, Piatetsky-Shapiro & Smyth, 1996) is "the nontrivial process of identifying valid, novel, potentially useful, and ultimately understandable patterns in data". It defines nine steps, usually grouped into five stages:

Stage Fayyad's steps In this notebook
0 · Domain & goals 1. Understand the application domain, prior knowledge and the end user's goals business context, two discovery goals, evaluation plan
1 · Selection 2. Create a target data set load both years, define discovery vs. validation periods
2 · Preprocessing 3. Data cleaning and preprocessing cancellations, non-product codes, invalid prices, duplicates, missing customers
3 · Transformation 4. Data reduction and projection customer RFM table (log, scaling, PCA); invoice × product basket matrix
4 · Data mining 5. Match goals to a mining method · 6. Choose algorithms · 7. Mine K-means segmentation · FP-Growth association rules
5 · Interpretation / Evaluation 8. Interpret mined patterns profile segments and rules; test them on the next year's data
→ Act 9. Act on the discovered knowledge consolidated outputs + a web app for marketing staff

Headline results: four customer segments that are stable (bootstrap ARI 0.94) and predict next year's behaviour — the top 17 % of customers ("Champions") produced 64 % of revenue and 96 % of them bought again the following year, against 40 % of "Lapsed one-off buyers". 579 association rules, of which 86 % meet the full thresholds again in the following year; the most useful are matching-design sets (e.g. red spotty paper napkins + cups → plates, 84 % confidence). Both are delivered in a web app for marketing staff.

How to run: Runtime → Run all (≈ 3–6 min on free Colab; most of it is downloading and reading the 44 MB Excel file once — later runs use a cache). Every figure, table and the app are written to artifacts/.

Stage 0 — Understanding the application domain and the KDD goals¶

Fayyad step 1: learn the domain and the relevant prior knowledge, and identify the end user's goals.

Domain and prior knowledge¶

The data come from a UK-based, store-less online retailer selling mainly unique all-occasion giftware (tableware, Christmas decorations, bags, children's items). Many customers are wholesalers who resell the products, so order sizes vary enormously, and sales are strongly seasonal, peaking in September–November ahead of Christmas. Chen, Sain & Guo (2012) first analysed the 2010-11 part of this data with RFM-based segmentation, which is the established retail practice:

  • RFM (recency, frequency, monetary value) is the standard, explainable way to group customers by purchasing behaviour; recent, frequent, high-spending customers are the most valuable and most likely to buy again.
  • Market-basket analysis (Agrawal et al., 1993) finds products bought together; it underpins "customers also bought" recommendations and store/catalogue layout.

End-user goals → discovery goals¶

End user Business goal KDD goal (descriptive, not predictive)
Marketing manager target campaigns at the right customers G1 — discover natural customer segments from purchasing behaviour
Merchandising / web team increase basket size with cross-selling G2 — discover product associations ("customers who buy X also buy Y")

How the patterns will be evaluated (Fayyad's four criteria)¶

Criterion Test used here
Valid patterns found in the discovery year must still hold in the following year (segments predict future spend; rules keep their lift and confidence)
Novel rules are split into obvious variants (same product, other colour/design) and genuinely cross-product associations
Potentially useful each segment gets a concrete action; validated rules feed a recommendation tool
Understandable segments described in plain words against customer tertiles; rules shown as readable product names

Fayyad step 2: select the data set, or subset of variables and records, on which discovery will be performed.

Target data set¶

Decision Choice Rationale
Records all transaction lines, Dec 2009 – Dec 2011 full history available
Attributes all 8 (invoice, product code, description, quantity, date, price, customer, country) all are needed for RFM and baskets
Discovery period 1 Dec 2009 – 30 Nov 2010 (12 months) one full seasonal cycle to mine patterns
Validation period 1 Dec 2010 – 9 Dec 2011 untouched year to test whether patterns are valid
Segmentation scope lines with a Customer ID RFM needs a customer
Basket scope all invoices (with or without Customer ID) an anonymous basket is still a basket

Stage 2 — Preprocessing¶

Fayyad step 3: basic operations such as removing noise, deciding how to handle missing data, and accounting for known changes.

df = raw.copy(); log = []
def step(action, mask_removed):
    global df
    log.append({"action": action, "lines_removed": int(mask_removed.sum()), "lines_left": int((~mask_removed).sum())})
    df = df[~mask_removed]

is_cancel = df["Invoice"].str.startswith("C")
cancellations = df[is_cancel].copy()                       # kept aside for a return-rate feature
step("Separate cancellation lines (invoice starts with 'C')", is_cancel)

# Remove purchases that were later cancelled in full (same customer, product and quantity)
cancel_keys = set(zip(cancellations["Customer ID"], cancellations["StockCode"], -cancellations["Quantity"]))
cancelled_purchase = pd.Series([k in cancel_keys for k in zip(df["Customer ID"], df["StockCode"], df["Quantity"])], index=df.index) & df["Customer ID"].notna()
step("Remove purchases matched by a later cancellation", cancelled_purchase)

non_product = ~df["StockCode"].str.match(r"^\d{5}")         # POST, DOT, M, BANK CHARGES, AMAZONFEE, TEST...
print("Non-product codes removed:", sorted(df.loc[non_product, "StockCode"].unique())[:25], "...")
step("Remove non-product codes (postage, fees, manual adjustments, tests)", non_product)
step("Remove lines with quantity <= 0 or price <= 0", (df["Quantity"] <= 0) | (df["Price"] <= 0))
step("Remove exact duplicate lines", df.duplicated())

# One description per product (codes have spelling variants / damaged-stock notes)
canonical = df.groupby("StockCode")["Description"].agg(lambda s: s.value_counts().index[0])
df["Description"] = df["StockCode"].map(canonical)
df["Revenue"] = df["Quantity"] * df["Price"]

preprocessing_log = pd.DataFrame(log); preprocessing_log.to_csv(REP / "preprocessing_log.csv", index=False)

Preprocessing decisions¶

  • Cancellations (19,494 lines) are separated, not netted. A cancellation is a different event from a purchase; netting would hide it. Purchases that were later cancelled in full (same customer, product and quantity — 13,653 lines) are removed so they don't count as demand. Partial returns cannot be matched this way; they are captured instead by each customer's return_rate.
  • Non-product codes (4,320 lines) — postage (POST, DOT), bank charges, Amazon fees, manual adjustments (M, ADJUST), samples, tests and DCGS… gift codes — are not products and would create meaningless rules ("postage → postage").
  • Zero/negative quantity or price (6,111 lines) are stock corrections, damaged/lost goods and free items, not sales.
  • Exact duplicates (33,203 lines) — identical invoice, product, quantity, price and timestamp — are treated as double entries. Baskets are binary, so rules are unaffected; monetary values shrink slightly.
  • Missing Customer ID (22.9 % of clean lines): kept for basket analysis (a basket is a basket), excluded from segmentation (RFM needs a customer). This is a limitation: if anonymous buyers behave differently, the segments describe registered customers only.
  • Extreme lines: the largest lines (e.g. 3,500 paper parasols for £8,925) look like genuine wholesale orders, not errors; they are kept because the log-transformation in Stage 3 limits their influence on clustering.

Result: 990,590 clean lines, 39,009 invoices, 4,699 products, 5,830 identified customers.

Stage 3 — Transformation¶

Fayyad step 4: find useful features to represent the data, using dimensionality reduction or transformation methods.

3.1 Customer table (for G1): RFM and behavioural features¶

In [7]:
def customer_features(lines, cancels, snapshot):
    """One row per customer, measured at `snapshot` (the day after the period ends)."""
    c = lines.dropna(subset=["Customer ID"]).groupby("Customer ID")
    f = pd.DataFrame({
        "recency_days": (snapshot - c["InvoiceDate"].max()).dt.days,
        "frequency": c["Invoice"].nunique(),
        "monetary": c["Revenue"].sum(),
        "tenure_days": (snapshot - c["InvoiceDate"].min()).dt.days,
        "distinct_products": c["StockCode"].nunique(),
        "country": c["Country"].agg(lambda s: s.mode()[0]),
    })
    f["avg_basket_value"] = f["monetary"] / f["frequency"]
    returned = (cancels.assign(v=-cancels["Quantity"] * cancels["Price"]).groupby("Customer ID")["v"].sum())
    f["return_rate"] = (returned.reindex(f.index).fillna(0) / f["monetary"]).clip(0, 1)
    return f

disc_lines, val_lines = df[df["InvoiceDate"] < DISCOVERY_END], df[df["InvoiceDate"] >= DISCOVERY_END]
disc_cancels = cancellations[cancellations["InvoiceDate"] < DISCOVERY_END]
customers = customer_features(disc_lines, disc_cancels, DISCOVERY_END)
print(f"{len(customers):,} customers in the discovery period"); display(customers.describe().T.round(1))

from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

SEGMENT_FEATURES = ["recency_days", "frequency", "monetary"]          # classic RFM - see the critic prompt about alternatives
projector = Pipeline([("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p)), ("scale", StandardScaler())])
Z = projector.fit_transform(customers[SEGMENT_FEATURES])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.5))
customers[SEGMENT_FEATURES].plot.box(ax=axes[0], logy=True, title="Raw RFM: heavily skewed (log axis)")
pd.DataFrame(Z, columns=SEGMENT_FEATURES).plot.box(ax=axes[1], title="After log1p + standardisation")
savefig("transformation_rfm")
print("Correlation of transformed RFM features:"); display(pd.DataFrame(Z, columns=SEGMENT_FEATURES).corr().round(2))
pca = PCA(2).fit(Z); print(f"2-D PCA projection keeps {pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum():.0%} of the variance (used for plots)")

Correlation of transformed RFM features:
recency_days frequency monetary
recency_days 1.00 -0.48 -0.43
frequency -0.48 1.00 0.81
monetary -0.43 0.81 1.00 
2-D PCA projection keeps 94% of the variance (used for plots)

Why these transformations. Frequency and monetary value span several orders of magnitude (1 to 172 orders; £2 to £319k per customer) and are right-skewed, while K-means uses Euclidean distance, so a handful of wholesalers would dominate untransformed data. log1p compresses the scale and standardisation gives each RFM dimension equal weight. Only three features are used so each segment can be explained in one sentence. Caveat: frequency and monetary still correlate at 0.81 after transformation, so purchase volume is effectively weighted twice — an iteration could drop one of them or cluster on principal components. The 2-D PCA projection keeps 94 % of the variance, so the plots in Stage 5 are faithful.

3.2 Basket matrix (for G2): invoice × product¶

In [9]:
item_name = df.drop_duplicates("StockCode").set_index("StockCode")["Description"]
dup = item_name.duplicated(keep=False)
item_name[dup] = item_name[dup] + " (" + item_name[dup].index + ")"        # keep labels unique

def item_support(lines):
    """Share of invoices that contain each product."""
    l = lines.assign(item=lines["StockCode"].map(item_name))
    return (l.groupby("item")["Invoice"].nunique() / l["Invoice"].nunique()).sort_values(ascending=False)

def basket_matrix(lines, items):
    """Boolean invoice x product matrix restricted to `items`; keeps EVERY invoice so support is relative to all baskets."""
    l = lines.assign(item=lines["StockCode"].map(item_name))
    b = l[l["item"].isin(items)].groupby(["Invoice", "item"]).size().unstack(fill_value=0) > 0
    return b.reindex(index=l["Invoice"].unique(), columns=items, fill_value=False)

disc_support = item_support(disc_lines)
frequent_items = disc_support[disc_support >= MIN_SUPPORT].index
disc_baskets = basket_matrix(disc_lines, frequent_items)
print(f"{disc_lines['Invoice'].nunique():,} invoices x {disc_lines['StockCode'].nunique():,} products -> reduced to {len(frequent_items)} products "
      f"with support >= {MIN_SUPPORT:.0%}; matrix {disc_baskets.shape[0]:,} x {disc_baskets.shape[1]} ({disc_baskets.values.nbytes / 1e6:.0f} MB)")
disc_support.head(15).sort_values().plot.barh(color="#55A868", title="Most frequently purchased products (share of invoices)")
savefig("transformation_item_support")

19,482 invoices x 4,047 products -> reduced to 717 products with support >= 1%; matrix 19,482 x 717 (14 MB)

Why this reduction is safe. An itemset can only be frequent if every item in it is frequent (the Apriori property). Removing the 3,330 products that appear in fewer than 1 % of invoices therefore loses no possible rule, and shrinks the matrix from 4,047 to 717 products (14 MB), which makes FP-Growth run in seconds. Every invoice is kept, so support is measured against all 19,482 discovery-year baskets.

Stage 4 — Data mining¶

Fayyad steps 5–7: match the goals to a mining method, choose the algorithms and parameters, and search for patterns.

Goal Method (step 5) Algorithm (step 6) Why
G1 segments clustering K-means on log-RFM fast, simple to explain, centroids are readable profiles; k chosen with silhouette + elbow
G2 associations association-rule mining FP-Growth + rule generation same output as Apriori but without candidate generation — much faster on wide baskets

4.1 Customer segmentation (step 7, G1)¶

In [10]:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

k_search = []
for k in range(2, 11):
    km = KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(Z)
    k_search.append({"k": k, "inertia": km.inertia_, "silhouette": silhouette_score(Z, km.labels_, sample_size=4000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)})
k_search = pd.DataFrame(k_search).round(4); k_search.to_csv(REP / "k_selection.csv", index=False)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(); ax.plot(k_search["k"], k_search["inertia"], marker="o"); ax.set(xlabel="k", ylabel="inertia (elbow)")
ax2 = ax.twinx(); ax2.plot(k_search["k"], k_search["silhouette"], marker="s", c="#C44E52"); ax2.set_ylabel("silhouette", color="#C44E52")
ax.set_title("Choosing the number of segments"); savefig("mining_k_selection")

K = int(k_search[k_search["k"].isin(K_RANGE)].sort_values("silhouette", ascending=False)["k"].iloc[0])
print(f"Chosen k = {K} (best silhouette within {list(K_RANGE)} - fewer than 3 segments is too coarse to act on)")

Chosen k = 4 (best silhouette within [3, 4, 5, 6] - fewer than 3 segments is too coarse to act on)
In [11]:
segmenter = Pipeline([("project", projector), ("kmeans", KMeans(K, n_init=20, random_state=RANDOM_STATE))]).fit(customers[SEGMENT_FEATURES])
customers["cluster"] = segmenter.predict(customers[SEGMENT_FEATURES])

# Stability: do bootstrap resamples find the same segments? (adjusted Rand index, 1 = identical)
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score
aris = []
for b in range(10):
    boot = customers.sample(frac=1, replace=True, random_state=b)
    m = Pipeline([("project", projector), ("kmeans", KMeans(K, n_init=10, random_state=b))]).fit(boot[SEGMENT_FEATURES])
    aris.append(adjusted_rand_score(customers["cluster"], m.predict(customers[SEGMENT_FEATURES])))
print(f"Bootstrap stability (ARI over 10 resamples): mean {np.mean(aris):.3f}, min {np.min(aris):.3f}")

Bootstrap stability (ARI over 10 resamples): mean 0.938, min 0.902

4.2 Association rules (step 7, G2)¶

In [12]:
from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import fpgrowth, association_rules
t0 = time.time()
itemsets = fpgrowth(disc_baskets, min_support=MIN_SUPPORT, use_colnames=True, max_len=3)
try:
    rules = association_rules(itemsets, num_itemsets=len(disc_baskets), metric="confidence", min_threshold=MIN_CONFIDENCE)
except TypeError:                                   # older mlxtend versions have no num_itemsets argument
    rules = association_rules(itemsets, metric="confidence", min_threshold=MIN_CONFIDENCE)
rules = rules[rules["lift"] >= MIN_LIFT].copy()
rules["antecedents"] = rules["antecedents"].apply(lambda s: tuple(sorted(s)))
rules["consequents"] = rules["consequents"].apply(lambda s: tuple(sorted(s)))
rules = rules.sort_values(["lift", "confidence"], ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"{len(itemsets):,} frequent itemsets -> {len(rules):,} rules with confidence >= {MIN_CONFIDENCE} and lift >= {MIN_LIFT} ({time.time() - t0:.0f}s)")
display(rules[["antecedents", "consequents", "support", "confidence", "lift"]].head(10).round(3))

5.1 Segment profiles (understandable)¶

In [13]:
# Critique fix: describe segments against customer TERTILES (a median split called a 2-order customer "frequent")
q = customers[SEGMENT_FEATURES + ["tenure_days"]].quantile([1 / 3, 2 / 3])
def level(v, col, low, mid, high):
    return low if v <= q.loc[1 / 3, col] else (high if v > q.loc[2 / 3, col] else mid)
def describe_segment(r):
    parts = [level(r["recency_days"], "recency_days", "active", "cooling", "lapsed"),
             level(r["frequency"], "frequency", "one-off", "repeat", "frequent"),
             level(r["monetary"], "monetary", "low-spend", "mid-spend", "high-spend")]
    return " · ".join(parts + (["new"] if r["tenure_days"] <= 90 else []))

prof = customers.groupby("cluster").agg(customers=("frequency", "size"), recency_days=("recency_days", "median"),
                                        frequency=("frequency", "median"), monetary=("monetary", "median"),
                                        avg_basket_value=("avg_basket_value", "median"), tenure_days=("tenure_days", "median"),
                                        return_rate=("return_rate", "mean"), revenue=("monetary", "sum"))
prof["revenue_share_%"] = (prof["revenue"] / prof["revenue"].sum() * 100).round(1)
prof["customer_share_%"] = (prof["customers"] / prof["customers"].sum() * 100).round(1)
prof = prof.sort_values("monetary", ascending=False)
prof["profile"] = prof.apply(describe_segment, axis=1)
prof["segment"] = [f"S{i + 1}" for i in range(len(prof))]
SEGMENT_OF = prof["segment"].to_dict(); customers["segment"] = customers["cluster"].map(SEGMENT_OF)
prof = prof.set_index("segment").round(2); prof.to_csv(REP / "segment_profiles.csv")

The segments are valid. Segments were built only from 2009-10 behaviour, yet they sharply separate who buys in 2010-11: 96 % of Champions bought again (median £2,558 each, 67 % of next year's revenue), against 74 % of S2, 66 % of New customers and 40 % of Lapsed one-off buyers (median £0). The ordering of the segments is exactly the ordering of their future value, so they capture something real about customers rather than noise. It also shows where marketing money matters: S2 still produced 21 % of next year's revenue, so reactivating "cooling" customers is worth more than chasing lapsed ones.

5.3 Are the rules valid? Re-measure each rule on the following year¶

In [17]:
val_baskets = basket_matrix(val_lines, items=frequent_items)
def rule_stats(baskets, a, c):
    has_a = baskets[list(a)].all(axis=1); has_c = baskets[list(c)].all(axis=1)
    sup_a, sup_c, sup_ac = has_a.mean(), has_c.mean(), (has_a & has_c).mean()
    conf = sup_ac / sup_a if sup_a else np.nan
    return pd.Series({"val_support": sup_ac, "val_confidence": conf, "val_lift": conf / sup_c if sup_c else np.nan})

rules = rules.join(rules.apply(lambda r: rule_stats(val_baskets, r["antecedents"], r["consequents"]), axis=1))
rules["holds_next_year"] = (rules["val_lift"] >= MIN_LIFT / 2) & (rules["val_confidence"] >= MIN_CONFIDENCE / 2)
print(f"{rules['holds_next_year'].mean():.0%} of rules still hold in the following year "
      f"(lift >= {MIN_LIFT / 2}, confidence >= {MIN_CONFIDENCE / 2})")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))
ax.scatter(rules["confidence"], rules["val_confidence"], c=rules["holds_next_year"].map({True: "#55A868", False: "#C44E52"}), s=12, alpha=.6)
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", lw=1); ax.set(xlabel="confidence, discovery year", ylabel="confidence, following year",
                                              title="Rule confidence: discovery vs following year")
savefig("evaluation_rule_validity")

99% of rules still hold in the following year (lift >= 1.5, confidence >= 0.2)

lift_ratio = (rules["val_lift"] / rules["lift"]).describe(percentiles=[.1, .5, .9]).round(2)
print(f"Strict test (lift >= {MIN_LIFT} and confidence >= {MIN_CONFIDENCE} again next year): "

5.4 Are the rules novel? Obvious variants vs cross-category associations¶

In [19]:
# Critique fix (novelty): a rule is an obvious VARIANT if all its products are the same product type that differ only in
# colour/design/size (e.g. KEY FOB GARAGE vs KEY FOB SHED); otherwise it links different product types (CROSS-PRODUCT).
STYLE = r"\b(RED|PINK|BLUE|GREEN|WHITE|BLACK|IVORY|CREAM|PURPLE|YELLOW|ORANGE|SILVER|GOLD|PASTEL|ASSORTED|ROSES|POLKADOT|RETROSPOT|SPOTTY|SPOT|STRIPES?|FLORAL|SMALL|LARGE|JUMBO|MINI|SET|OF|AND|THE|WITH|DESIGN|\d+)\b"
words = lambda name: re.findall(r"[A-Z]{2,}", re.sub(STYLE, " ", name.upper()))
def same_product(a, b):
    wa, wb = words(a), words(b)
    if len(wa) >= 2 and len(wb) >= 2 and (wa[:2] == wb[:2] or wa[-2:] == wb[-2:]):
        return True
    sa, sb = set(wa), set(wb)
    return len(sa & sb) / max(len(sa | sb), 1) >= 0.5

from itertools import combinations
rules["rule_type"] = rules.apply(lambda r: "variant (same product, other design)"
                                 if all(same_product(a, b) for a, b in combinations(r["antecedents"] + r["consequents"], 2))
                                 else "cross-product", axis=1)
display(rules.groupby("rule_type").agg(rules=("lift", "size"), median_lift=("lift", "median"),
                                       holds_strict_pct=("holds_strict", lambda s: round(s.mean() * 100, 1))))
show = ["antecedents", "consequents", "support", "confidence", "lift", "val_confidence", "val_lift"]
print("Strongest cross-product rules that met the full thresholds again in the following year:")
display(rules[(rules["rule_type"] == "cross-product") & rules["holds_strict"]][show].head(14).round(3))
rules.to_csv(REP / "association_rules_evaluated.csv", index=False)

Evaluation against the Stage 0 criteria¶

Criterion Evidence Verdict
Valid Segments: next-year activity 96 % / 74 % / 66 % / 40 %, in the predicted order; bootstrap ARI 0.94. Rules: 86 % meet the full thresholds (lift ≥ 3, confidence ≥ 0.4) again next year; median lift changes by only +5 %. ✅
Novel 425 of the 579 rules (73 %) are obvious variants (same product, other colour/design) — expected, and still useful for "complete the set" prompts. The 154 cross-product rules (75 % of which hold strictly next year) reveal that customers buy matching-design sets across product types (red spotty napkins + cups → plates; polkadot bowls → cups) and themed bundles (vintage Christmas napkins → Christmas cake cases). The "new customer" segment (S3) was not anticipated by a plain RFM view. ✅ partly
Potentially useful Each segment has an action; 396 strictly validated rules drive the recommendation tab of the app. ✅
Understandable Segments described in plain words against tertiles; rules shown as product names with confidence and lift. ✅

Iterations made (KDD loops back): the first evaluation used median-split labels (mislabelling S3 as "frequent"), lenient validity thresholds (99 % "held") and a word-matching novelty test that called key-fob variants cross-category. All three were corrected after the critic review — see critiques/round_1.md.

Step 9 — Acting on the discovered knowledge¶

Fayyad step 9: use the knowledge directly, incorporate it into another system, or document and report it. Patterns are re-mined on both years (now validated) and delivered as a lookup app for marketing and merchandising staff.

In [20]:
import joblib
snapshot = df["InvoiceDate"].max().normalize() + pd.Timedelta(days=1)
final_customers = customer_features(df, cancellations, snapshot)
final_segmenter = Pipeline([("project", Pipeline([("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p)), ("scale", StandardScaler())])),
                            ("kmeans", KMeans(K, n_init=20, random_state=RANDOM_STATE))]).fit(final_customers[SEGMENT_FEATURES])
final_customers["cluster"] = final_segmenter.predict(final_customers[SEGMENT_FEATURES])

# Align final clusters with the validated discovery segments (same names S1..Sk) via nearest centroids
disc_c = segmenter.named_steps["kmeans"].cluster_centers_
fin_c = final_segmenter.named_steps["kmeans"].cluster_centers_
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment
cost = ((fin_c[:, None, :] - disc_c[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(-1)
rows, cols = linear_sum_assignment(cost)
final_map = {int(r): SEGMENT_OF[int(c)] for r, c in zip(rows, cols)}
final_customers["segment"] = final_customers["cluster"].map(final_map)

full_support = item_support(df)
fb = basket_matrix(df, full_support[full_support >= MIN_SUPPORT].index)
fi = fpgrowth(fb, min_support=MIN_SUPPORT, use_colnames=True, max_len=3)
try:
    final_rules = association_rules(fi, num_itemsets=len(fb), metric="confidence", min_threshold=MIN_CONFIDENCE)
except TypeError:
    final_rules = association_rules(fi, metric="confidence", min_threshold=MIN_CONFIDENCE)
final_rules = final_rules[final_rules["lift"] >= MIN_LIFT]
final_rules = final_rules.assign(antecedent=final_rules["antecedents"].apply(lambda s: " + ".join(sorted(s))),
                                 consequent=final_rules["consequents"].apply(lambda s: " + ".join(sorted(s))))
validated = {(" + ".join(r["antecedents"]), " + ".join(r["consequents"])) for _, r in rules[rules["holds_strict"]].iterrows()}
final_rules["validated_next_year"] = [(a, c) in validated for a, c in zip(final_rules["antecedent"], final_rules["consequent"])]

out_rules = final_rules[["antecedent", "consequent", "support", "confidence", "lift", "validated_next_year"]].sort_values("lift", ascending=False).round(4)
out_rules.to_csv(APP / "rules.csv", index=False)
final_customers.reset_index().to_csv(APP / "customer_segments.csv", index=False)
joblib.dump(final_segmenter, APP / "segmenter.joblib")
meta = {"created": datetime.now().isoformat(timespec="seconds"), "k": K, "segment_features": SEGMENT_FEATURES,
        "snapshot": str(snapshot.date()), "segments": SEGMENT_ACTIONS, "cluster_to_segment": {str(k): v for k, v in final_map.items()},
        "profiles": prof.drop(columns="revenue").reset_index().to_dict(orient="records"),
        "versions": {"python": platform.python_version(), "numpy": np.__version__, "pandas": pd.__version__, "scikit-learn": sklearn.__version__}}
(APP / "metadata.json").write_text(json.dumps(meta, indent=2, default=str))
print(f"{len(final_customers):,} customers segmented | {len(out_rules):,} rules ({out_rules['validated_next_year'].sum():,} validated) | snapshot {snapshot.date()}")

    products = sorted(set(" + ".join(rules["antecedent"]).split(" + ")))
    product = st.selectbox("Customer has this product in the basket", products)
    only_valid = st.checkbox("Only rules that met the full thresholds again in the following year", value=True)
    hits = rules[rules["antecedent"].apply(lambda a: product in a.split(" + "))]
    if only_valid:
        hits = hits[hits["validated_next_year"]]
    if hits.empty:
        st.info("No strong associations for this product.")
    else:
        st.dataframe(hits[["antecedent", "consequent", "confidence", "lift"]].head(15), hide_index=True)
        top = hits.iloc[0]
        st.success(f"Suggest **{top['consequent']}** — bought in {top['confidence']:.0%} of baskets containing "
                   f"{top['antecedent']} ({top['lift']:.1f}x more often than average).")
with lookup:
    cid = st.text_input("Customer ID", value=customers["Customer ID"].iloc[0])
    row = customers[customers["Customer ID"] == cid.strip()]
    if row.empty:
        st.warning("Customer not found.")
    else:
        r = row.iloc[0]; s = seg_info[r["segment"]]
        st.subheader(s["name"]); st.write(f"**Recommended action:** {s['action']}")
        c1, c2, c3 = st.columns(3)
        c1.metric("Days since last order", int(r["recency_days"])); c2.metric("Orders", int(r["frequency"])); c3.metric("Spend (GBP)", f"{r['monetary']:,.0f}")
with new_cust:
    c1, c2, c3 = st.columns(3)
    rec = c1.number_input("Days since last order", 0, 1000, 30)
    freq = c2.number_input("Number of orders", 1, 500, 3)
    mon = c3.number_input("Total spend (GBP)", 1.0, 1e6, 500.0)
    cluster = int(segmenter.predict(pd.DataFrame([{"recency_days": rec, "frequency": freq, "monetary": mon}]))[0])
    seg = meta["cluster_to_segment"][str(cluster)]
    st.subheader(seg_info[seg]["name"]); st.write(f"**Recommended action:** {seg_info[seg]['action']}")
with overview:
    st.dataframe(pd.DataFrame(meta["profiles"]), hide_index=True)
"""
(APP / "app.py").write_text(APP_CODE.strip() + "\n")
v = meta["versions"]
(APP / "requirements.txt").write_text(f"streamlit\nscikit-learn=={v['scikit-learn']}\nnumpy=={v['numpy']}\npandas\njoblib\n")
compile(APP_CODE, "app.py", "exec")
print("App files:", sorted((p.name, f"{p.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB") for p in APP.iterdir()))
print(f"When deploying, choose Python {v['python'][:4]} so the pinned versions install and the segmenter loads.")

When deploying, choose Python 3.13 so the pinned versions install and the segmenter loads.

Consolidating the knowledge¶

  • Agreement with prior knowledge: the segments match classic RFM intuition — a small group of recent, frequent buyers carries most revenue (17 % of customers → 64 % of revenue) — which builds trust in the result.
  • What is new: design collections cross product types. For a giftware merchandiser this suggests organising the web shop by collection (all "red retrospot" items together) as well as by product type, and bundling matching items.
  • Conflicts to watch: the strongest "rules" are colour variants; promoting them only helps if the product page doesn't already show all colours.
  • Maintenance: sales are highly seasonal and the range changes each year (only 717 of 4,047 products reach 1 % support), so segments and rules should be re-mined quarterly, and rules re-validated before Q4.
